summary: Defines an optional attribute syntax called collection for IPP. A collection is a container that holds one or more named member attributes, which allows printing options to be grouped. It updates RFCs 2910 and 2911 and was replaced by RFCs 8010 and 8011.

eli5.summary: A collection is a labeled box that holds several settings together, like a lunchbox holding a sandwich and fruit. It lets printing options be bundled in the protocol.

questions: what is an ipp collection attribute
how are ipp member attributes grouped
how are collections encoded in ipp
subtitle: A container for grouping related printing options together in the Internet Printing Protocol.

tldr.problem: The Internet Printing Protocol (IPP) lacked a way to group related attributes of different types together, making it hard to bundle printing options like media color and size as a unit.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC adds a new optional attribute syntax called 'collection' that acts as a container holding one or more named member attributes. Collections work like a dictionary or Map in programming languages.
tldr.outcome: Printing clients and servers can now group related settings together while remaining backward compatible with older IPP implementations. This was later consolidated in RFC 8010 and RFC 8011.

facts.label: Member flexibility
facts.value: Members can be any IPP attribute syntax type

today: RFC 3382 defined the optional collection syntax for IPP/1.0 and IPP/1.1. Collections were later consolidated and refined in RFC 8010 and RFC 8011, which unified and updated the IPP specification.

sections.title: The Problem with Flat Attributes
sections.content:
The Internet Printing Protocol (IPP) Model and Semantics supports most common data structures from programming languages, but it lacks a way to group several attributes of different types together. For example, specifying media (paper) in IPP required clients to send separate attributes for media type, color, and size, without a clear way to say that these properties belonged together or to bundle them as a unit.

The IPP community recognized that programming languages solve this problem with structures: Java uses Map, PostScript uses dictionaries. Without a similar mechanism, IPP had no standard way to represent related attributes as a group. This made printer configuration verbose and ambiguous: when a client specified color and size separately, was it asking for any combination of those values, or only certain combinations?
sections.eli5: Imagine ordering from a restaurant without a menu. You would have to say 'I want white bread, I want lettuce, I want tomato' separately. A collection is like being able to say 'I want a sandwich' and have the ingredients grouped together.

sections.title: Collections as Containers
sections.content:
A collection is an attribute syntax that holds one or more named values called member attributes. Each member attribute can have any IPP attribute syntax type, and can be either single-valued or multi-valued (a set of values). Collections themselves can be single-valued (one collection) or multi-valued (1setOf collection, meaning a set of collections). Member attributes within a collection may be marked as required or optional for the printer to support and for the client to supply.

Collections can also be nested: a member attribute can itself be a collection, creating a hierarchy. For example, a 'media-col' (media collection) could contain a 'media-size' collection, which in turn contains integer dimensions. The member attributes within a collection may appear in any order, and the printer is free to reorder them when storing or returning the collection.
sections.eli5: A collection is like a labeled box. Inside, you can put several items in any order. You can even put smaller boxes inside the big box. The printer remembers what label goes on the box.

sections.title: Defining a Collection Attribute
sections.content:
When a specification document defines a collection attribute, it must follow strict rules to ensure compatibility and clarity. The document must name the collection, specify whether it is single-valued or multi-valued, list all mandatory and optional member attributes, and describe the semantics and supported values of each member. The document must also define three related attributes: a -default attribute giving the default collection value, a -supported attribute listing the supported member attributes or enumerating all supported collection values, and optionally a -ready attribute listing available values that require no human intervention.

Member attribute names must be unique within their collection, and the rules for naming allow member attributes to reuse the names of existing IPP attributes (with the same syntax), use names that could appear elsewhere in IPP, or be unique to the collection. This flexibility lets different collections share member attribute names without conflict, while also allowing collection-specific names when needed.
sections.eli5: When you define a new collection type, you have to write down what box you are making, what items go in it, which items are required, and what values each item can have. You also have to say what the default is and what the printer has ready.

sections.title: Encoding Collections on the Wire
sections.content:
Collections are encoded in IPP messages using three new tags: 'begCollection' (0x34) marks the start of a collection, 'endCollection' (0x37) marks the end, and 'memberAttrName' (0x4A) precedes the name of each member attribute within the collection. Each member attribute is encoded as a pair of values: first, a memberAttrName tag with the attribute's name, followed by the attribute's value using its own attribute syntax. If a member attribute is multi-valued, its multiple values follow before the next memberAttrName. Nested collections follow the same pattern, with begCollection and endCollection tags delimiting the nested structure.

This encoding ensures backward compatibility with IPP 1.0 and 1.1 parsers that do not support collections. An older parser sees the begCollection and endCollection tags as unknown attribute syntaxes and ignores the entire collection and its member attributes. The 'memberAttrName' tag and the sequence structure make collections look like a single-valued attribute containing a set of values, so an old parser gracefully skips over them without confusion.
sections.eli5: On the wire, a collection looks like: 'begin collection named media-col, then attribute name is media-color, its value is blue, then attribute name is media-size, value is a nested collection with x=6 and y=4, then end collection.' Old printers do not understand the markers, so they just skip the whole thing.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility and Conformance
sections.content:
Collections are designed as an optional extension to IPP. A printer or client that does not support the collection syntax can still operate with clients and printers that do. When an older printer receives a request containing a collection attribute it does not understand, the begCollection tag appears to be an unknown attribute syntax, and the entire collection is treated as an unsupported attribute. The printer returns the name of the unsupported collection in the Unsupported Attributes group, allowing the client to retry without the collection attribute.

When a collection attribute is partially unsupported (only certain member attributes are not recognized), the printer returns a collection containing only the unsupported member attributes, marked with the 'unsupported' value. This precise handling allows for graceful degradation: clients and printers can negotiate which collection features are supported and adapt their behavior accordingly.
sections.eli5: If your old printer does not know what a collection is, it just says 'I do not understand media-col' and gives the job back to the client. The client can then try again without the collection. It is like speaking to someone who does not understand one of your words: you just do not use that word.
